title: Best AWS Database Cost Management Tools in 2026: What to Use for RDS Spend
summary: One platform to monitor, optimize, and manage your cloud. No engineering required. #GetPumped
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


-


**Native AWS tools** are best for inspecting your AWS bill first.[AWS’s optimization guide](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/aws-tools-to-optimize-your-amazon-rds-costs) describes dashboards that show database spend by purchase option, instance type, and daily storage cost.


-


**Pump** is best if you want cost visibility and eligible commitment management in one free platform.[Pump View](https://www.pump.co/view) provides forecasts, budgets, and anomaly alerts; use a billing-data demo to confirm RDS charge detail and Database Savings Plan support.


-


**DoiT** is best when missing tags make cost attribution difficult. It also offers commitment management, but requires a quote and proof of RDS-specific coverage.


-


**nOps** is best if AWS commitment management is the priority. Its savings-based fee needs a clear baseline, and RDS-specific coverage needs a demo.


-


**CloudZero** is best for allocating cloud costs to products or customers. Its spend-based subscription supports analysis rather than RDS workload changes; verify charge-level detail in a demo.


## Why RDS spend is harder to control than EC2


An RDS total can hide which charge you can reduce.[AWS prices database instances, storage, provisioned IOPS, applicable I/O requests, and backup storage](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/pricing/) under different conditions.[RDS Proxy adds a separate charge](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/proxy/pricing/) when you use it. A lower instance price will not address excess provisioned IOPS or backup storage.[AWS’s RDS optimization guide](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/aws-tools-to-optimize-your-amazon-rds-costs) treats those costs differently, recommending IOPS monitoring and backup retention controls.


RDS discounts also require a different check from EC2 discounts. RDS Reserved Instances apply to matching database instances under one- or three-year terms.[Database Savings Plans](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/introducing-database-savings-plans-for-aws-databases/) use a one-year hourly spending commitment for eligible database usage, but eligibility varies by configuration.[Compute Savings Plans](https://aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/pricing/) cover EC2, Fargate, and Lambda, not RDS. Before you count a proposed discount as savings, check which RDS usage qualifies and which charges remain on the bill.


## The RDS bill-component checklist


Before comparing tools, separate the charges on your bill using[AWS RDS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/pricing/) as a checklist. A reduction in instance hours will not necessarily reduce storage or backup charges.


-


**Instance hours.** Check the database instance type and hours billed. Stopping an instance pauses its instance-hour charges, but other charges can continue.


-


**Provisioned storage.** Check allocated storage separately. Storage remains billable while the instance is stopped.


-


**Provisioned IOPS.** Check whether your storage configuration includes separately billed IOPS. AWS charges for provisioned capacity even when you use fewer IOPS, and that charge can persist during a stop.


-


**I/O requests.** Check for request charges where they apply, including magnetic RDS storage and Aurora. Do not assume every RDS database pays a per-request fee.


-


**Backup storage.** Compare backup usage with your retention policy. Backup charges can continue while an instance is stopped, and[AWS’s optimization guide](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/aws-tools-to-optimize-your-amazon-rds-costs) explains how backup lifecycle settings can remove unneeded copies.


-


**RDS Proxy.** Check[proxy pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/proxy/pricing/) as a separate charge. AWS meters provisioned-instance proxies by vCPU-hour and Aurora Serverless proxies by capacity-unit hour. Confirm whether a proxy remains active before assuming its charge stops with a database.


Discounts need a separate check. RDS Reserved Instances offer one- or three-year terms for matching instance configurations, not a blanket discount on the bill. AWS says some RDS usage may qualify for a one-year Database Savings Plan, but the supplied AWS sources do not verify eligibility for your exact SKU or for storage, I/O, backups, or proxy.[Compute Savings Plans pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/pricing/) names EC2, Lambda, and Fargate, so do not count on one to cover RDS. Verify each proposed discount against current AWS eligibility documentation before including it in a savings estimate.


## How to evaluate a database cost tool


Start with the RDS charges you need to control.[AWS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/pricing/) separates instance usage, storage, provisioned IOPS, applicable I/O requests, backup storage, and RDS Proxy charges. Ask each vendor to show those charges in your billing data. A dashboard that reports total RDS spend may help you spot a change, but it cannot tell you which charge caused it.


Compare three capabilities separately. Reporting shows where you spend money. Commitment management purchases or manages eligible discounts against usage. Instance-level control starts, stops, or resizes databases. A tool may offer one capability without the others, so a savings claim should identify which action produces the savings and which charges it affects.


Treat a capability as documented here when the vendor’s own product documentation or pricing page states it. If those sources do not confirm RDS charge-level reporting, a specific database commitment, or a pricing model, mark it as a question to test with your billing data. Ask the vendor to demonstrate the feature and reconcile its projected savings with your AWS bill before you commit.


## Native AWS tools (Cost Explorer, Trusted Advisor, CUDOS, Compute Optimizer)


**Best for** You can use native AWS tools to establish an RDS cost baseline before paying for another tool. They give you billing data and recommendations, but you still need to check which charges drive each database’s spend.


**What it is** Cost Explorer shows AWS spending trends, while Trusted Advisor checks for issues such as idle or underused DB instances. CUDOS, an AWS dashboard built on Cost and Usage Report data, lets you examine database spending by purchase option, instance type, and daily storage cost. CloudWatch adds usage and billing metrics.[AWS’s RDS optimization guide](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/aws-tools-to-optimize-your-amazon-rds-costs) documents those Trusted Advisor, CUDOS, and CloudWatch uses. Confirm Compute Optimizer’s current RDS coverage in its own documentation before relying on it for database recommendations.


**Pros** The underlying billing data lets you investigate instance, storage, provisioned IOPS, applicable I/O request, and backup charges separately rather than treating RDS as one cost.[RDS Proxy has separate pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/proxy/pricing/) , so include its charges in that review. CloudWatch can show whether a database uses the capacity you provisioned, but its billing metrics do not replace a charge-level billing breakdown.


**Cons** CUDOS requires you to work with billing data, and CloudWatch usage signals require interpretation before you change a database configuration. These tools provide visibility and recommendations. The listed tools do not automatically stop or resize RDS instances or manage commitment purchases across accounts. AWS offers a separate Instance Scheduler solution for scheduled start and stop actions.


**Pricing** Start with the AWS tools available under your existing account and support plan, then check the costs of the services you use to build dashboards or query billing data. The Trusted Advisor checks available to you depend on your AWS Support plan.


### Pump


**Best for.** Pump fits you if you want to assess cloud spend and eligible commitment savings in one free platform without adding a software subscription. Your team retains control of RDS instance changes.


**What it is.**[Pump View](https://www.pump.co/view) combines cloud cost and usage data with reports, forecasts, budgets, and anomaly alerts. Pump Save can manage eligible commitments when configured. Ask Pump to show which RDS charges View separates and which database commitments Save supports using your own bill.


**Pros.** Pump combines spend reporting and eligible commitment management without a platform fee. A free estimate using read-only access or a billing CSV lets you check the proposed savings against your AWS bill before you decide whether the platform fits. Ask for a demo of the exact RDS charge breakdown you need.


**Cons.** Pump's published View page does not confirm that level of RDS charge detail. Pump Save's support for AWS Database Savings Plans and specific RDS Reserved Instances also needs confirmation. Pump does not start, stop, or resize instances, so you must handle those changes elsewhere.


**Pricing.**[Pump is free to use](https://pump.co/) . Start with a free savings estimate using read-only access or a billing CSV, then confirm which proposed savings apply to eligible RDS usage.


### DoiT


**Best for.** DoiT suits you if you need to attribute cloud costs without relying on consistent resource tags.


**What it is.** DoiT provides cloud cost allocation and commitment management. Its[buyer guide](https://www.doit.com/blog/cloud-cost-management-tools-buyers-guide) says its PerfectScale for Commitments product automates AWS Database Savings Plans. Treat that as a vendor claim and ask DoiT to demonstrate coverage for your eligible database usage.


**Pros.** Tagging-free allocation can help you account for spending when resources have missing or inconsistent tags. DoiT also serves a large customer base, though customer count alone does not establish how well it handles your RDS bill.


**Cons.** DoiT's broader allocation and advisory offering may be more than you need if the immediate job is checking RDS charges and eligible discounts. Its cited guide does not establish the RDS charge-level breakdown you need. Ask DoiT to demonstrate that breakdown and its database commitment coverage using your bill.


**Pricing.** DoiT describes a spend-based pricing model, but its guide does not establish your contract rate. Request a quote alongside a billing-data demonstration.


### nOps


**Best for.** nOps suits you if commitment management is your priority and you want cost visibility across multiple clouds.


**What it is.**[nOps describes](https://www.nops.io/blog/aws-cost-management-tools/) AWS commitment management alongside visibility across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.


**Pros.** Its commitment tools can help you manage covered spend without relying only on manual purchases.


**Cons.** The cited nOps guide does not establish RDS charge-level reporting or Database Savings Plan support. Ask for a billing-data demonstration, and include the percentage-of-savings fee when comparing its projected net savings with other options.


**Pricing.** nOps says it charges a percentage of realized savings after a free savings analysis. Confirm which savings count toward the fee and how nOps calculates them.


### CloudZero


**Best for** CloudZero suits you if you need to attribute cloud spending to customers or products and understand which parts of your business incur the cost.


**What it is**[CloudZero describes](https://www.cloudzero.com/blog/cloud-cost-management-tools/) a cost intelligence platform that allocates spending across multiple business dimensions. You can use those views to investigate who owns a charge, rather than relying on an account-level total.


**Pros** Multi-dimensional allocation can help you connect shared database spending to the customers or products that use it.


**Cons** CloudZero describes its focus as cost intelligence rather than workload automation. Its documented allocation strengths do not establish a separate breakdown of RDS instance, storage, IOPS, applicable I/O request, backup, and RDS Proxy charges. If RDS savings are the immediate goal, test that breakdown and factor its subscription into the decision.


**Pricing** CloudZero describes a spend-based platform subscription. Confirm the rate and contract terms with CloudZero.

## Run a billing-data proof-of-concept before you commit


Start with one recent billing period and give each vendor the same read-only access or billing CSV. Ask for an RDS savings estimate broken out by instance hours, storage, provisioned IOPS, applicable I/O requests, backup storage, and RDS Proxy. Compare those figures with your bill before accepting a total savings number.


Ask the vendor to show which charges each recommendation changes. An instance commitment, for example, should not appear to reduce backup or storage charges unless the vendor can explain and document that effect. Check the assumed workload, discount eligibility, existing commitments, and any vendor fees. Keep projected savings separate from savings already visible on a bill.


If the tool cannot trace its estimate to specific charges and assumptions, treat the number as unverified. For a low-commitment starting point,[Pump](https://pump.co/) offers a free initial savings estimate in about two minutes using read-only access or a billing CSV. Use its report as you would any vendor’s estimate and check the proposed savings against your own RDS bill.


## FAQs


**How do RDS Reserved Instances, Database Savings Plans, and Compute Savings Plans differ?**[RDS Reserved Instances](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/pricing/) apply to matching instances on one- or three-year terms.[Database Savings Plans](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/introducing-database-savings-plans-for-aws-databases/) use a one-year hourly spending commitment for eligible database usage, but you must check eligibility for your specific RDS usage.[Compute Savings Plans](https://aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/pricing/) cover EC2, Fargate, and Lambda, not RDS.


**Can a cost tool stop or resize RDS instances automatically?** Some tools can take operational action. For example,[AWS Instance Scheduler](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/aws-tools-to-optimize-your-amazon-rds-costs) can start and stop tagged RDS instances, but Pump does not start, stop, or resize them.


**What do “documented” and “unverified” mean in this guide?** “Documented” means a vendor’s own product documentation or pricing page supports the stated capability. “Unverified” means you should test the claim, such as a tool’s ability to separate RDS charge types, against your billing data before buying.


**How should I read a vendor’s savings percentage?** Ask which charges and baseline the percentage covers. Compare the projected savings with your actual bill after commitment costs and vendor fees, rather than applying the percentage to all RDS spend.


## Choosing the right tool for your RDS spend


Choose a tool based on the work you need done. Native AWS tools or a cost-visibility platform can help you find which RDS charges drive spend. Commitment-management tools suit eligible, predictable usage, while a consulting service may fit if you need help planning changes across accounts.


Start by testing each provider's estimate against the same AWS bill.[Pump offers a free savings estimate](https://pump.co/) using read-only access or a billing CSV, so you can assess eligible opportunities without paying for a platform subscription. Confirm the RDS charges and discounts behind any projected savings before making a commitment.
